item.title: Michigan ‘Let’s Go Blue’ Songwriters Countersue Over ‘Shockingly Low’ Video Game Sync
item.description:
[Intro music plays]
Host: Welcome to this week's entertainment news update. We're diving into a fascinating lawsuit that's making waves in the music industry. Imagine writing a fight song for your university's marching band, only to find yourself in a battle over the song's ownership decades later. That's exactly what's happening with the composers of the University of Michigan's iconic "Let's Go Blue" song.
[Music transitions to a brief clip of "Let's Go Blue"]
Host: Albert Ahronheim and Joe Carl co-wrote "Let's Go Blue" back in the 1970s as Michigan students. But now, they're facing off against publishers Theodore Presser and Carl Fischer in a lawsuit over who owns the song's composition rights. The publishers claim they've owned the rights since 1978 and even licensed the song to Electronic Arts for use in the College Football video game series.
[Music transitions back to the podcast theme]
Host: However, Ahronheim and Carl tell a different story. They say they exercised their termination rights under copyright law years ago, regaining control of the song's publishing. But they allegedly discovered that Presser and Fischer had secretly licensed the song to EA for just $1,000. The composers are now seeking financial damages and a judge's declaration that they're the rightful owners of "Let's Go Blue".
[Music transitions to a brief clip of a court gavel]
Host: The case hinges on the technicalities of termination rights, a provision of copyright law that allows authors to reclaim their intellectual property after signing it away. Ahronheim and Carl claim they followed the proper procedures, but the publishers argue that they failed to make an official report to the U.S. Copyright Office, rendering their termination notice invalid.
[Music transitions back to the podcast theme]
Host: This lawsuit is just one of many currently testing the limitations of termination rights. Other notable cases involve Salt-N-Pepa, Universal Music Group, and even a ruling that termination rights can't be invoked due to a bankruptcy filing. We'll be keeping an eye on this developing story and bringing you updates as more information becomes available.
[Outro music plays]
Host: Thanks for tuning in to this week's entertainment news update. Join us next time for more exciting stories from the world of music, film, and beyond.
